## First Official Celebration

On February 2, 1887, Groundhog Day was officially celebrated for the first time at Gobbler's Knob in Punxsutawney, Pennsylvania. However, Groundhog Day first appeared in Punxsutawney's local paper in 1886, when the Punxsutawney Spirit newspaper printed the news of the first observance in 1886.

## Origins and Organization

The first official celebration in 1887 was organized by a local newspaper editor named Clymer Freas, who convinced a group of hunters and businessmen, who called themselves the Punxsutawney Groundhog Club, to trek to a spot called Gobbler's Knob.

## Historical Context

The tradition has deeper roots: The holiday began as a Pennsylvania German custom in southeastern and central Pennsylvania in the 18th and 19th centuries, and has its origins in ancient European weather lore, wherein a badger or sacred bear is the prognosticator as opposed to a groundhog.

## Philadelphia as Temporary Capital

Philadelphia served as the nation's capital until 1800, when the federal government moved to its permanent home in Washington, D.C. More specifically, Congress Hall, located in Philadelphia at the intersection of Chestnut and 6th Streets, served as the seat of the United States Congress from December 6, 1790, to May 14, 1800.

## How Philadelphia Became the Temporary Capital

With a vote of 38 to 22, Members chose Philadelphia as an interim capital, largely because the city served as the social, financial, cultural, and geographic center of the young nation which stretched the eastern seaboard. The Residence Act also declared Philadelphia to be the temporary capital for a period of ten years.

## Move to Washington, D.C.

On November 17, 1800, Congress moved to Washington from Philadelphia, convening in the newly completed north wing of the unfinished Capitol. The Residence Act of July 16, 1790, put the nation's capital in current-day Washington as part of a plan to appease pro-slavery states who feared a northern capital as being too sympathetic to abolitionists.

## The Battle of Hastings (1066)

On 14 October 1066, the Battle of Hastings was fought between the army of Harold Godwinson, the last of the Anglo-Saxon kings, and William, Duke of Normandy, in a decisive event in the conquest of England. Two great armies prepared to fight for the throne of England, with Harold's forces on a hilltop 7 miles from Hastings, while Duke William of Normandy's troops faced them from across a valley below.

Victory at Hastings was not certain until dusk, some nine hours after the fighting began—an indication of how evenly matched and led the two armies were. At the end of the fierce battle, William of Normandy's men were victorious, Harold Godwinson was dead, his troops routed, and the road to London was wide open. On 25 December 1066 William was crowned King of England in Westminster Abbey.

## The Bayeux Tapestry

The Bayeux Tapestry is a band of embroidered linen from the Middle Ages depicting more than 70 scenes with Latin inscriptions of the Norman Conquest of England in 1066. It measures 224 feet (68.3 meters) long and approximately 20 inches (50 centimeters) wide.

In one of the Bayeux Tapestry's most famous scenes, Harold is shown wounded in the face by an arrow. The Bayeux Tapestry is a primary source of historical information for the period and has been remarkably well preserved throughout its nine-hundred year history.

## Genera of Colosteidae

The genera within Colosteidae include Colosteus (type genus), Deltaherpeton, Greererpeton, Ichthyerpeton, and Pholidogaster.

## Taxonomic Classification

Colosteidae was named by Cope (1875), and its type is Colosteus.

The taxonomic placement of Colosteidae has been revised over time: It was assigned to Ganocephala by Cope (1875); to Phyllospondyli by Kuhn (1946); to Colosteoidea by Carroll (1988); to Temnospondyli by Gauthier et al. (1989); and to Tetrapoda by Clack and Milner (2015).

## General Description

Colosteidae is a family of stegocephalians (stem-group tetrapods) that lived in the Carboniferous period. They are now considered to be part of a lineage intermediate between the earliest Devonian terrestrial vertebrates (such as Ichthyostega), and the different groups ancestral to all modern tetrapods, such as temnospondyls and reptiliomorphs.

Based on the web search results, here's what I found about the Pruett rule and blue moon definition:

## Pruett Rule Definition

Pruett's rule defines a blue moon as the second full moon in a calendar month. This is the most common meaning today.

## How It Works

The duration between two full moons is approximately 29.5 days, which is less than the length of a typical calendar month, making it possible for two full moons to fall in a single calendar month, with the second one called a blue moon.

## Frequency

A "Pruett" blue moon happens about every 2 years, 8 months, and 18 days on average. Additionally, sometimes two "Pruett" blue moons can even happen in a single year, like in 1915, 1961, 1999, 2018, and 2037.

## Historical Origin

An amateur astronomer named James Hugh Pruett helped make the idea of the second full moon in a month being "blue" popular in 1946. Interestingly, the modern definition most people know today actually stems from a well-documented misinterpretation when writer James Hugh Pruett, in the March 1946 issue of Sky & Telescope, incorrectly described the definition used by the Maine Farmers' Almanac.

## Displacement to Reserves

The Hän were forcibly moved out of their traditional hunting grounds and into a reserve to make way for the prospectors, who exploited the land by cutting down much of the timber and leaving the land's former inhabitants without resources and stricken by poverty.

## Devastating Consequences

The native Hän people had been forced onto a reserve, but suffered from the introduction of new diseases like Smallpox, and the ecosystem was devastated by the mining efforts, and the Hän hunting and fishing grounds were destroyed. By 1904 they needed support from the NWMP to prevent famine.

## Government Response

When the Han people in the Klondike were relocated to a reserve shortly after the gold rush began, the Dominion government gave them no assistance.

## Broader Context

Where in southern Canada the creation of reserves acted to remove Indigenous peoples from land desired for settlement and agriculture, colonizers in the Yukon displaced Indigenous peoples from traditional territory to claim the land for mining.

## Early Contact History

The Han were notably one of the last Northern Athabaskan groups to encounter Europeans. After Campbell's initial visit, sustained contact developed slowly. Two trading posts were established in the 1870s:

Bishop William Bompas later introduced Anglican Christianity to the region, further transforming Han society and religious practices.

results:
Based on the search results, here's what causes pernicious anemia and its connection to vitamin deficiency:

## The Vitamin Connection

Pernicious anemia is an autoimmune condition that prevents your body from absorbing vitamin B12. It is the most common cause of vitamin B12 deficiency in developed countries.

## How It Develops

The anemia is caused by vitamin B12 deficiency secondary to intrinsic factor (IF) deficiency. IF is a glycoprotein produced and secreted by parietal cells that binds B12 and facilitates its transport to the terminal ileum for absorption.

The body's immune system attacks cells in the stomach that make a substance called intrinsic factor. Without this substance, the intestines can't take in B-12.

## Impact on Red Blood Cells

Without adequate vitamin B12, you have fewer red blood cells carrying oxygen throughout your body. Left untreated, pernicious anemia can cause serious medical issues, including irreversible damage to your nervous system.

## What is Betanin?

Betanin, which is extracted from red beetroots, is a commonly used natural red food colour. Betanin (C24H27N2O13) is a water-soluble red pigment that occurs in the roots of beetroot, Beta vulgaris L.

## Food Additive Status

As a food additive, its E number is E162. According to the regulation on food additives betanin is permitted quantum satis as a natural red food colorant (E162). Additionally, as a food additive, betanin has no safety concerns.

## Color Properties

The color of betanin depends on pH; between pH four and five, it is bright bluish-red, becoming blue-violet as the pH increases. Once the pH reaches alkaline levels, betanin degrades by hydrolysis, resulting in a yellow-brown color.

## Applications

Betanin, obtained from beetroot, particularly Beetroot Red, is an approved red food colorant and is widely used in the food industry to color food products and beverages in pink, red, or purple colors. The most common uses of betanins are in coloring ice cream and powdered soft drink beverages.

## Stability Challenges

Betanin degrades when subjected to light, heat, and oxygen; therefore, it is used in frozen products, products with short shelf life and products sold in dry state.

Mudhoney is a 1965 Southern Gothic film directed by Russ Meyer, based on the novel Streets Paved With Gold (1958) by Raymond Friday Locke. It's a melodramatic tale about a drifter who falls in love with his employer's married niece, a beautiful young woman with an abusive, alcoholic husband.

Raymond Friday Locke served as both the author of the novel and a screenwriter for the film adaptation, which also starred Hal Hopper, Antoinette Christiani, John Furlong, and Rena Horten.

Summer surface air temperatures during 2023 were the warmest ever observed in the Arctic. More specifically, the summer Arctic average temperature was the warmest on record at 43 degrees Fahrenheit (6.4 Celsius).

The shallow seas around the margins of the Arctic Ocean have warmed dramatically in the past four decades, with these areas having warmed around 2 degrees C (nearly 4 degrees F) over the satellite era, part of a feedback loop in which warming air and water temperatures shrink the sea ice cover, which exposes more of the ocean to direct sunlight, which drives more warming.

Polytrichum piliferum belongs to the Kingdom Plantae, Division Bryophyta, Class Polytrichopsida, Order Polytrichales, Family Polytrichaceae, and Genus Polytrichum.

**Species Overview:**

Polytrichum piliferum, commonly known as the bristly haircap, is an evergreen perennial species of moss in the family Polytrichaceae. The bristly haircap moss is small-sized to medium-sized and forms loose tufts with wine-reddish stems.

The most distinguishing feature of P. piliferum is the long, white awn at the tips of the leaves, and it is the only species in its genus where the awn is completely hyaline.

## History and Founding

In 1843, Jewish residents of Hartford and New Haven successfully petitioned the Connecticut General Assembly to allow Jews to form congregations, build synagogues, and worship openly. Soon after, a small group of German-speaking Jews in Hartford began to meet in homes, and in 1876, the young Congregation Beth Israel built a synagogue on Charter Oak Avenue in Hartford. Rev. Isaac Meyer was the first Rabbi of the Congregation.

## History

The congregation was founded in Philadelphia in 1847 and is recognized as the sixth-oldest Reform congregation in the country. Orthodox in observance at first, KI adopted reform in 1855, and thus became the first progressive congregation in Philadelphia, and only the fifth in the entire country, to take the way of radical experimentation. By 1900, it had become one of the largest Reform congregations in the United States.

## Notable Rabbis

Since appointing its first rabbi in 1861, the congregation has been led by eight rabbis, including David Einhorn, Joseph Krauskopf, Bertram Korn, and Simeon Maslin, who served as president of the Central Conference of American Rabbis from 1995 to 1997.

More specifically:

- David Einhorn, one of the greatest Jewish intellectuals of his day, a firebrand abolitionist and author of the prayer book which formed the original basis of the Union Prayer Book, was the Rabbi from 1861 to 1866.

- He was succeeded by Dr. Samuel Hirsch, the former Chief Rabbi of Luxembourg, who was both a scholar and a pioneer in Jewish social services in Philadelphia.

- Dr. Krauskopf, a member of the first graduating class of the Hebrew Union College, followed Dr. Hirsch, and under Dr. Krauskopf, KI became the largest synagogue in the United States.

## Location

The synagogue occupied several locations in Philadelphia before constructing a building on North Broad Street in 1891. In 1956, the congregation relocated to its current site in Elkins Park.

Based on the search results, the intertidal region is divided into three zones: low, middle, and high, based on the overall average exposure of the zone.

Here are the characteristics of each zone:

1. **High Intertidal Zone**: Only covered by the highest of the high tides, and spends much of its time as terrestrial habitat. It is inhabited by hardy sea life that can withstand pounding waves, such as barnacles, marine snails, mussels, limpets, shore crabs, and hermit crabs.

2. **Mid Intertidal Zone**: Regularly exposed and submerged by average tides. The tides ebb and flow twice a day, and it is inhabited by a greater variety of both plants and animals, including sea stars and anemones.

3. **Low Intertidal Zone**: Only exposed to air at the lowest of low tides and is primarily marine in character. It is virtually always underwater except during the lowest of spring tides, and life is more abundant there because of the protection provided by the water.

results:
I found comprehensive information about *Ixodes scapularis* life cycle and Lyme disease transmission timing. Here's a summary of the key findings:

## Life Cycle Overview

*Ixodes scapularis* has a three-stage life cycle (larva, nymph and adult) that spans 2 years. The cycle begins when females typically lay eggs in the late spring but hatched larvae do not seek hosts actively until months later, in summer.

## Nymph Stage and Spring Activity

After blood-feeding, larvae over-winter and molt to nymphs. Nymphs begin host-seeking in the spring with peak activity typically observed from May through July, depending on location. This nymph stage is particularly significant for disease transmission: although ticks at any of these three stages are competent vectors for *B. burgdorferi* transmission to humans, most cases of Lyme disease result from the bite of the 2-3 mm nymphal tick.

## Adult Season

After blood-feeding, nymphs molt to adults and seek hosts in the fall. Adults are active mainly in the fall and spring, but can be active also in the winter months in settings where daytime temperatures are above freezing and there is little to no snow cover.

## Disease Transmission Context

In the northern parts of the tick's range, *I. scapularis* nymphs are considered the primary vectors of the agents causing Lyme disease, anaplasmosis and babesiosis. The nymph's small size and spring-summer activity make it the most significant stage for human disease transmission.

## Primary Etymology

The name Baghlan is possibly derived from the Bactrian term bagolango, meaning "image-temple", which originates from the Old Iranian root baga danaka, referring to a sanctuary or divine shrine, inscribed on the temple of Surkh Kotal during the reign of the Kushan emperor Kanishka in the early 2nd century CE. The Chinese Buddhist monk Xuanzang traveled through Baghlan in the mid-7th century CE, and referred to it as the "kingdom of Fo-kia-lang".

Based on the search results, here's what we know about the Mount Vesuvius eruption date:

## The Traditional Date

The date of August 24th is widely accepted in the literature, deriving from a medieval translation of Pliny the Younger's letter, which has been questioned several times since the 17th century.

## Recent Evidence Challenging August 24

New evidence challenges the traditional 24 August date for Vesuvius's eruption in 79 CE, pointing instead to mid-autumn based on artifacts, coins, and graffiti.

The key finding is a charcoal inscription discovered in 2018. A handwritten charcoal inscription was found on an interior wall in Pompeii's Regio V, dated "XVI K(alendas) Nov(embris)", meaning "the 16th day before the Kalends of November", which would be the 17th of October by modern reckoning. Because the writing was done in charcoal, which is fragile and easily erasable, archaeologists believe it was likely written shortly before the eruption and not long before being buried by ash.

## Current Scholarly Consensus

The balance of evidence now points to the autumn, perhaps October 24, as the most likely date for Mt. Vesuvius's eruption. However, scholars disagree over whether the eruption occurred in summer or fall, and why the debate may never be settled.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about the origin of tennis:

The sport originated in French monasteries around the year 1000, making **France** the country where tennis was first played. The monks played a game called jeu de paume, "game of the hand," in which they used their hand to hit a wooden ball over a rope stretched across the courtyard.

Historians believe that the name "tennis" came from the French term tenez, meaning "take this!" During the game, the monks would shout, 'tenez!' as they served the ball.

The game evolved significantly over time. Over the next several hundred years, the game spread throughout Europe, becoming extremely popular with the nobility. By the 13th century, there were as many as 1,800 courts in France. In the 16th century, a racket was introduced to hit the ball instead of using the hand, and the game also began to take on its unique scoring system.

The modern form of tennis that we know today, however, originated in England. The modern version of tennis, often referred to as "lawn tennis," originated in England in the late 19th century. Major Walter Clopton Wingfield is credited with popularizing the game in 1873.

## Architectural Style

Big Ben and Elizabeth Tower were designed in the Gothic Revival style of architecture. The main characteristics of this design type include lancet windows, heavy ornamentation, pinnacles, and the use of natural materials such as stone and iron.

## Design Details

The design of Big Ben, spearheaded by architect Augustus Pugin, draws on various elements of Gothic architecture, such as pointed arches, spires, and intricate decorative stonework. Big Ben features many of these attributes, most notably a 115-foot iron-framed spire topped with a pinnacle. The tower also features tall and narrow windows referred to as lancet windows, as well as limestone cladding typical of the medieval era.

## Construction Materials

The bottom 200 feet (61.0 m) of Elizabeth Tower's structure consists of brickwork with sand coloured Anston limestone cladding. The remainder of the tower's height is a framed spire of cast iron.

The Elizabeth Tower stands 96 metres (315 feet) tall and was designed in the Gothic Revival style, harmonising beautifully with the façades of the Palace of Westminster.

## Origins and Early Examples

The earliest documented example of the revived use of Gothic architectural elements is Strawberry Hill, the home of the English writer Horace Walpole. This whimsical villa was built in Twickenham between 1749–1776.

## The Movement's Development

The Gothic Revival was a conscious movement that began in England to revive medieval Gothic forms, from the second half of the 18th century and throughout the 19th century. By the early 1800s, scholarship on medieval Gothic was growing, and a more archaeological approach emerged, including an increasing interest in preserving and restoring older buildings.

## Key Pioneers

Augustus Welby Northmore Pugin (1812-1852) was the key protagonist for the Gothic Revival by much of Victorian England. By the nineteenth century, Gothic Revival had become a popular architectural form for public buildings like the Palace of Westminster, designed by architects Sir Charles Barry and A.W.N. Pugin.

## American Gothic Revival

American architects introduced Gothic Revival buildings in the mid-19th century, inspired by an 18th-century British revival. The first American Gothic house was by Alexander Jackson Davis in Baltimore, MD in 1832, and Davis was the first American architect to promote the Gothic style, particularly in his book "Rural Residences".

# Coronet Records Australia Label Design

The distinctive feature of Coronet Records Australia's label design was its **octagonal shape**. According to the article, the label "was recognizable by its octagonal label," which differentiated it from the standard circular record labels of the era.

# Coronet Records Summary

The Wikipedia article describes **three separate record companies** that operated under the Coronet Records name:

1. **San Francisco (1940s)**: Produced Dave Brubeck's first recordings before folding due to financial difficulties. Its catalog was absorbed by Fantasy Records.

2. **United States (1950s-1960s)**: A Premier Albums division releasing budget LP records. It notably re-released material from The Four Lovers, leading to a 1966 lawsuit when "the label used their images and likenesses to misportray the records as being from The Four Seasons."

3. **Australia (early 1950s-1962)**: Based in Sydney, this label was "recognizable by its octagonal label." It functioned as the principal house label for the Australian Record Company until CBS Records acquired ARC in 1960. The octagonal-labeled Coronet was phased out in January 1963, replaced by CBS Australia's "walking eye" branding.

The octagonal label design was the distinctive visual identifier for the Australian operation, setting it apart from standard record labels of the era.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about Nauru's geology related to volcanoes:

## Nauru's Volcanic Geology

From mid Eocene (35 Ma) to Oligocene times a submarine volcano built up over a hotspot and formed a seamount composed of basalt. The seamount rises over 4300 m above the ocean floor.

However, it's important to note that Nauru does **not** have active volcanoes currently. The volcano was eroded to sea level and a coral atoll grew on top to a thickness of about 500 m. The coral was raised above sea level about 30 metres and is now a dolomite limestone outcrop which was eroded in classic karst style into pinnacles up to 20 metres high.

The volcanic seamount underlying Nauru is an ancient formation from the Eocene-Oligocene period (approximately 35 million years ago). Today, Nauru exists as a raised coral atoll sitting atop this long-extinct submarine volcano, rather than as an active volcanic island.

## Major Volcanic Fields in Syria

Syria has 4 Pleistocene volcanoes. The primary volcanic features in Syria include several significant volcanic fields:

**Jabal al-Druze**: The Jabal al-Druze volcanic field, the southernmost in Syria, lies in the Haurun-Druze Plateau in SW Syria near the border with Jordan, with the most prominent feature being 1800m-high Jabal al-Druze. The alkaline volcanic field consists of a group of 118 basaltic volcanoes active from the lower-Pleistocene to the Holocene.

**Es Safa**: The Es Safa volcanic field, in southern Syria SE of the capital city of Damascus, consists of a lava field with broad areas containing Holocene volcanic vents. Al-Safa had a last eruption around 1850 AD.

**Harrat Ash Shaam**: The massive Harrat Ash Shaam volcanic province extends from Syria through Jordan and into northern Saudi Arabia, containing many smaller volcanic fields.

**Other Fields**: Other fields include the Golan Heights and the Kra Lava Field where radiocarbon dating indicated an eruption at 2,670 BCE ± 200 years.

Most of Syria's volcanic activity is historical rather than currently active, with a boiling lava lake reported in the Es Safa volcanic area in the middle of the 19th century.

The timelines don't directly overlap in a traditional sense. Based on the search results, here's what we know about when calculus was invented:

Newton's formative period for his research on calculus was from 1665 to 1670, while Leibniz worked a few years later, in the 1670s. More specifically, Isaac Newton began developing his version of calculus around 1665–1666, during his "year of wonders" when he returned to his family estate in Lincolnshire to escape the bubonic plague ravaging Cambridge.

Leibniz performed the research himself, devised this idea in the mid-1670s, and published his work in 1684. In contrast, Newton published his work in 1671, while Leibniz published his work in 1684.

Today, the consensus is that Leibniz and Newton independently invented and described calculus in Europe in the 17th century. So while Newton developed calculus first (1665-1670), Leibniz developed it independently a few years later (1670s) and was actually the first to publish his work on the subject.

## Key Facts

The Bath School bombing in 1927 remains the deadliest school massacre in U.S. history. The final death toll from the Bath school disaster was 45 people: 38 children and seven adults, including Kehoe.

The bombings constituted the deadliest act of mass murder in a school in U.S. history, claiming more than three times as many victims as the Columbine High School massacre.

## The Attack

Andrew Kehoe assimilated himself into the school board and volunteered to do maintenance work at the school. He spent months lacing well over 500 pounds of dynamite and pyrotol in the basement. On the day of the massacre, he used rigged explosives to destroy the buildings of his nearby farm moments before the explosives in the school were detonated by an alarm clock at 9:45 am.

## Motivation

The attack was executed by a former school board member, Andrew Kehoe, who was seeking revenge for losing an election. Bath raised property taxes to pay for it. As a farmer and treasurer of the township school board, Kehoe was not happy with the decision.

Here are the key details about the 1920 Wall Street bombing:

On September 16, 1920, a horse-drawn wagon loaded with dynamite and iron weights exploded on the corner of Wall Street and Broad Street in New York City, killing 38 people and injuring hundreds more.

The bombing was ultimately decided to have been an act of terrorism performed by "Reds"—anarchists and communist sympathizers—who wanted to shatter the symbols of American capitalism. A stack of anarchist flyers found in a mailbox a block away from Wall Street supported this theory.

The case was never solved. A subsequent FBI investigation in 1944 concluded that the explosion was likely the work of Italian anarchists or terrorists, but no individual was ever charged.

## Murray State University Presidents and the Seventh President

In 1983, Kala Stroup was elected the 7th President of Murray State, marking her as the first woman to hold the presidency at the University and within Kentucky's higher education system. As the first female President of Murray State University Dr. Kala M. Stroup oversaw the opening of the National Scouting Museum of the Boy Scouts of America on Murray's campus.

Kala M. Stroup served as president of Murray State University from 1983 to 1990. Prior to serving as president at Murray State she served as Vice President for Academic Affairs at Emporia State University and held several administrative positions at the University of Kansas.

### Other Presidents in the University's History

## Land Donation

Most of the lands of Neshaminy State Park were donated to the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania by the estate of Robert R. Logan in 1956. Logan was a descendant of James Logan who was the colonial secretary to William Penn the founder of Pennsylvania. The property had been a wedding gift to Robert Logan and his wife, the former Sarah Wetherill of Philadelphia, by the bride's parents.

## Colonial History

The area's history extends back much further than the 1956 donation. William Penn had what many people considered a crazy idea—he would buy the land from its current inhabitants, the American Indians. During 1682, William Penn made his first purchase from the Lenape chiefs. The land was bounded on the south by Neshaminy Creek. A year later, Penn's second purchase was bounded on the north by Neshaminy Creek, making what is now Neshaminy State Park the core of the future Commonwealth of Pennsylvania.

## Phoenix Open Golf - Winners History

The tournament has been known by many names over its nearly 90-year history, including the Western Open, the Arizona Open, the Ben Hogan Invitational, the Phoenix Open, the FBR Open and now the WM Phoenix Open. The Phoenix Open began in 1932, but due to lack of local support, the tournament was discontinued after the 1935 event. The tournament was revived thanks to the energy and vision of one man, Bob Goldwater, Sr.

## Notable Multiple Winners

Four players have won this event on three different occasions: Gene Littler (1955,1959,1969), Arnold Palmer (1961,1962,1963), Mark Calcavecchia (1989,1992,2001), and Phil Mickelson (1996,2005, 2013).

## Key Findings

Damon Hill clinched his only F1 drivers' championship on October 13, 1996, at the Japanese Grand Prix at Suzuka. The British racer became the first driver in F1 history to follow in their parent's footsteps and become a champion child of another title-winning driver. He followed in the footsteps of his father Graham Hill, who had been champion in 1962 and 1968.

The Williams FW18 car, powered by Renault, looked like the class of the field. Seven victories in the opening 11 races put him in control of the championship heading into the final round at Suzuka, holding a nine-point advantage over rookie teammate Jacques Villeneuve.

The season concluded in Japan with Damon Hill needing a composed drive to secure the 1996 championship, and he drove flawlessly to take his eighth and most crucial victory. Villeneuve took pole but made a poor start and later retired when a wheel detached from his car.

He remained the only driver to achieve this distinction for many years, until Nico Rosberg, son of 1982 World Champion Keke Rosberg, matched the feat in 2016.

## Brown Rhinoceros Beetle (Xylotrupes gideon)

The brown rhinoceros beetle or fighting beetle, Xylotrupes gideon, is a species of large scarab beetle belonging to the subfamily Dynastinae.

### Size and Length

Xylotrupes gideon can reach a length of 3.5–7 centimetres (1.4–2.8 in). More specifically, these are large beetles, with sizes ranging from about 35 - 70mm for most individuals. As usual with rhinoceros beetles there is a great difference between the genders. Males are larger than females.

### Other Characteristics

These beetles are shiny dark red, dark brown, or black in coloration. They have two chitinous bifurcated horns, a thick thoracic horn and a smaller cephalic horn, which they use to eliminate their rivals during the mating period.

This species can be found across much of Southeast Asia, south to Australia and east to the Solomon Islands.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about bark/barque as a large sailing ship type:

A barque (or bark) is a type of sailing vessel with three or more masts of which the fore mast, mainmast, and any additional masts are rigged square, and only the aftmost mast (mizzen) is rigged fore and aft. 

Despite being larger, barques actually required smaller crew to manage and control the ship. This sail configuration is considered to be the best possible compromise between a full-rigged ship and a ship rigged entirely with fore and aft sails.

Historically, by the 16th century, during the Age of Exploration, Portuguese shipbuilders developed larger barques suited for transoceanic voyages. In the 18th and 19th centuries, barques became a staple of merchant fleets, naval services, and exploratory missions due to their cargo capacity and seaworthiness.

results:
Here's information about the Crab Nebula supernova remnant:

## Overview
The Crab Nebula is the shattered remnant of a massive star that ended its life in a massive supernova explosion. Nearly a thousand years old, the supernova was noted in the constellation of Taurus by Chinese astronomers in the year 1054 AD.

## Location and Size
The nebula is about 6,500 light-years away from the Earth, and is 5 light-years across.

## Current Structure
The much fainter remnant observed today is an expanding shell of gas and dust, and outflowing wind powered by a pulsar, a rapidly spinning and highly magnetized neutron star. The nebula, 6,500 light-years away, is expanding at 1,100 km (700 miles) per second.

## Composition and Features
The blue region traces the cloud of energetic electrons trapped within the star's magnetic field, emitting so-called "synchrotron" radiation. The orange filaments are the tattered remains of the star and consist mostly of hydrogen. Green is singly ionized sulfur, and red indicates doubly ionized oxygen. These elements were expelled during the supernova explosion.

## Type of Supernova
In June 2021, scientists announced they'd finally found evidence for a new type of supernova, an electron-capture supernova. Consequently, they now believe the Crab nebula may be this type of supernova.

Based on the search results, here's the history of the dam's two official names:

## Origins of the Names

Boulder Dam was originally named after the canyon in which the dam was considered to be the best place for it to be located, with surveyors originally suggesting the dam be constructed at Boulder Canyon, leading the initiative to be called the Boulder Canyon Dam Project. However, geologic research conducted as early as 1921 showed that this location was actually far from ideal, and Black Canyon later was deemed to be a better location.

## The 1930 Naming as Hoover Dam

When work on the dam began in 1930 with the completion of the railroad connecting Black Canyon to Las Vegas, Secretary of the Interior Ray Lyman Wilbur officially named the dam after President Hoover. Although it did not gain traction or the support he thought it would, and locally was rarely referred to as that.

## Reversion to Boulder Dam

Hoover lost the next election to Franklin Delano Roosevelt and in 1933 the name reverted back to Boulder Dam. Franklin Roosevelt's Secretary of the Interior, Harold Ickes, changed the name back to Boulder Dam, and the name Hoover also had many negative connotations because his administration coincided with the onset of the Depression.

## 1947 Official Renaming

On 30th April 1947, the 80th Congress passed legislation to officially designate the dam, previously known as Boulder Dam, to be "Hoover Dam" in honor of President Herbert Hoover.

Based on the search results, I can provide you with information about Ursula Le Guin's short stories and their relationship to the Earthsea world:

Nine short stories by Le Guin are set in Earthsea; the earliest two ("The Word of Unbinding" and "The Rule of Names") were published in her 1975 collection of short stories The Wind's Twelve Quarters, five in Tales from Earthsea, and the final two (2014's "The Daughter of Odren" and 2018's "Firelight") in an illustrated collection in The Books of Earthsea (released in 2018 to celebrate the 50th anniversary of A Wizard of Earthsea).

The stories in Tales from Earthsea range from a few hundred years before A Wizard of Earthsea to just before The Other Wind, and feature some of Le Guin's most popular characters, including the Wizard Ged himself. 

However, it's worth noting that these short stories were written and published after "A Wizard of Earthsea" (published in 1968), rather than before. While the original trilogy of Earthsea books—A Wizard Of Earthsea, The Tombs Of Atuan, and The Farthest Shore—were published in 1968-1972, Tales From Earthsea was published in 2001. The short stories set in Earthsea were thus developed and added to the world after the initial novel, even though many of them are set chronologically earlier in the Earthsea world.

## African Bush Elephant is the Largest

The African savanna elephant is the largest elephant species, compared to the Asian elephant. Full grown bulls weigh over 10 tonnes and stand 4 meters tall and 7 meters long. More specifically, males can weigh up to 7 tonnes (7,000 kg) and reach a maximum height of 13 feet at the shoulder.

results:
Here's a summary of the discovery and history of these three anti-leprosy drugs:

## Dapsone
In the 1940s, dapsone was used to treat leprosy, making it the first antibiotic to be widely used for leprosy treatment in the 1950s. However, by the 1960s, the M.leprae bacteria had started to develop resistance to dapsone monotherapy.

## Rifampicin and Clofazimine
The search for additional anti-leprosy drugs led to the use of clofazimine and rifampicin in the 1960s and 1970s. More specifically, in the early 1960s, rifampicin and clofazimine were discovered and subsequently added to the treatment regimen.

## Multidrug Therapy
In response to dapsone resistance, scientists developed a new multi-drug regimen of dapsone added to other drugs: rifampicin and clofazimine. The World Health Organization (WHO) formally recommended the new triple-drug protocol in 1981, and since 1981, the WHO has provided Multi Drug Therapy (MDT) across the world free of cost.

**Discovery of Rifamycins:**
The rifamycin complex derived from Nocardia mediterranei was first discovered in 1957. Rifamycins were first isolated from a fermentation culture of Streptomyces mediterranei, with about seven rifamycins discovered, named Rifamycin A, B, C, D, E, S, and SV.

**Synthesis of Rifampicin:**
Rifampicin was synthesized in 1965 and its antimicrobial profile described in 1966. Rifampicin was first synthesized in 1965 at Lepetit Pharmaceuticals in Milan, Italy.

**Key Researchers:**
The initial discovery of the rifamycin family was led by Piero Sensi and Maria Teresa Timbal at Lepetit Pharmaceuticals.

**Nature of the Compound:**
Rifampicin is a semisynthetic drug resulting from extensive structural manipulations designed to render rifamycin SV more bioavailable. After successful clinical trials, rifampicin was introduced into therapeutic use in 1968.

Clofazimine was synthesized in 1954 by Vincent C. Barry and co-workers at Trinity College, Dublin. Initially known as B663, it was first synthesized in 1954 by Barry et al. as an anti-tuberculosis drug.

Clofazimine is a red-colored synthetic derivative of riminophenazines initially isolated from lichens. Being initially developed as an anti-tuberculosis treatment, it was repurposed for the treatment of leprosy, prior to re-positioning for the treatment of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis and other infections. Specifically, the drug was thought to be ineffective against tuberculosis but in 1959 Chang demonstrated its effectiveness against leprosy. After clinical trials the product was launched in 1969 as Lamprene.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about the snake that killed Cleopatra:

## The Snake Identification

According to the most widely repeated theory of Cleopatra's death, she died from a venomous snake bite, inflicted either by an asp (a small viper) or an Egyptian cobra. More specifically, the name 'asp' was often used for various kinds of snake in ancient times, and it was also the specific name for the poisonous Egyptian cobra.

## The Legend

According to legend, Cleopatra killed herself by clutching an asp to her bosom and letting it bite her. The asp was a symbol of royalty to the Egyptians, while the cobra was associated with Cleopatra's favorite goddess, Isis.

## Modern Skepticism

However, solid historical evidence relating to Cleopatra's death is thin, as those who compiled the most comprehensive accounts of her life, notably the Roman writer Plutarch, lived generations after her death. Cobras were typically at least five feet long, and could grow up to eight feet; much too large to smuggle into Cleopatra's mausoleum in a basket of figs, as the story goes.

Some modern scholars suggest alternative methods of death, such as poison, but the Egyptian cobra remains the most famous version of the Cleopatra death legend.

## Jimmy Carter

During his presidency, Jimmy Carter created 39 national park units. In partnership with his interior secretary Harold Ickes, FDR created 140 wildlife refuges, 29 national forests, and 11 national monuments. He also created several new national parks, including Isle Royale National Park, Joshua Tree, the Dry Tortugas, and the Channel Islands.

In terms of national parks specifically, Jimmy Carter created more national park units (39) than FDR. However, FDR's conservation efforts were more broadly focused across multiple categories of protected lands, including wildlife refuges and national forests.

The first edition was published in 1735. This folio volume of only 11 pages presented a hierarchical classification, or taxonomy, of the three kingdoms of nature: stones, plants, and animals. Each kingdom was subdivided into classes, orders, genera, species, and varieties.

The grey parrot was formally described in 1758 by Swedish naturalist Carl Linnaeus in the tenth edition of Systema Naturae. He placed it with all other parrots in the genus Psittacus and coined the binomial name Psittacus erithacus.

The City of London Police was formed during 1839, ten years after the Metropolitan Police, with the first Commissioner, Daniel Whittle-Harvey, being responsible for around 500 officers.

However, there's some important context to this date. Reform of the City Police began in 1832 when a daytime duty of 1 Superintendent, 3 Inspectors, 10 Sergeants and 85 constables was established. In 1839 the City of London Police Act was passed, changing the name of the London City Police, established in 1832, to the City of London Police.

The creation of the force came about because when Sir Robert Peel established the Metropolitan Police in 1829 The City of London resisted his attempts to consolidate the policing of The City and greater London with one force. Instead, the City chose to continue with traditional Constables to enforce the law in the one square mile.

## Category Overview

The Grammy Award for Best Metal Performance recognizes artistic excellence in a metal performance by a solo artist, collaborating artists, established duo, or established group. The Best Metal Performance category was first presented at the 32nd Annual Grammy Awards in 1990.

## Most Decorated Artists

Tool has received the award three times. Black Sabbath, Nine Inch Nails, Ozzy Osbourne and Slayer have each received the award twice.

- Ministry holds the record for the most nominations without a win, with six, while Megadeth holds the record for most nominations before their first win, winning on their 10th nomination.

## Legion of Honour Models and Variations

The models belonged to the First Empire, Type I, are divided into four Types according to the statute's changes: Type I (1804-1806); Type II (1806); Type III (1806-1808); and Type IV (1808-1813).

There are known four models: "Large Head", "Small Head", and Biennais model. The Biennais model are known since 1806.

## Hanging Device and Crown Details

In Type IV, the versions between 1808-1813 have surmounted large crown with two points affixed suspension on the top arm. There are extremely rare versions that featured eagles on the crown suspension; however, they are different eagles from the Second Empire.

All grades feature ball finials.

There is a great deal of variation of these Order; the following variables may be encountered: size; composition; manufacturer; medallion; inscription punctuation; surmounting crown or wreath; enameled wreath suspension.

## Higher-Level Classification

Cannabis belongs to Kingdom Plantae, Clade Tracheophytes, Clade Angiosperms, Clade Eudicots, Clade Rosids, and Order Rosales. The family Cannabaceae is known as the hemp family and includes about 170 species grouped in about 11 genera, including Cannabis (hemp), Humulus (hops) and Celtis (hackberries).

## Genus and Species

The species Cannabis sativa L. belongs to the genus Cannabis, which belongs to the Cannabaceae family. However, there is some taxonomic debate at the species level. The taxonomy of the genus Cannabis is contentious. Many experts assert that the genus has only a single species, Cannabis sativa, with a number of varieties or subspecies. Others hold that there are two or three species: C. sativa and C. indica, and sometimes C. ruderalis, based on differences in plant stature, branching patterns, geographic origin, and cannabinoid profiles.

## Historical Context

Martynov elevated Cannabis and Humulus to a family rank, and coined the name Cannabaceae. Not until the mid-20th century has Cannabaceae come into common usage.

## Plant Family

The raspberry plant belongs to the Rosaceae family, which is also known as the rose family. The rose family consists of more than 2,830 different plant species, many of them being actual rose varieties.

## Genus and Scientific Name

Raspberries belong to the Rubus genus. Rubus idaeus is the scientific name of the raspberry plant.

## Complete Taxonomic Classification

The full taxonomic hierarchy for raspberry species follows this structure:

Kingdom: Plantae; Clade: Tracheophytes; Clade: Angiosperms; Clade: Eudicots; Clade: Rosids; Order: Rosales; Family: Rosaceae; Genus: Rubus

## Subgenus

Taxonomists recognize 12 subgenera within Rubus, but only the raspberries (idaeobatus) and blackberries (Eubatus) have obtained commercial significance.

## Related Species

The raspberry plant family includes other common fruits such as apple, strawberry, and pear.

Based on the search results, here's the taxonomy and classification of the mulberry plant:

## Family: Moraceae

Moraceae is a family of flowering plants comprising about 48 genera and over 1100 species, and is commonly known as the mulberry or fig family. The mulberry family occurs primarily in tropical and semi-tropical regions, and includes a wide variety of herbs, shrubs, and trees, characterized by a milky sap and reduced, unisexual flowers.

## Higher Taxonomic Classification

The genus Morus belongs to the Kingdom Plantae, Order Rosales, and Family Moraceae. More specifically, mulberry belongs to the order Rosales, family Moraceae, and genus Morus.

## Genus: Morus (True Mulberries)

Mulberry is the common name for any of the deciduous trees comprising the genus Morus of the flowering plant family Moraceae, characterized by simple, alternate leaves, a milky sap, and a small, edible, multiple fruit.

## Species Complexity

Over 150 species names have been published, and although differing sources may cite different selections of accepted names, fewer than 20 are accepted by the vast majority of botanical authorities. Morus classification is further complicated by widespread hybridisation, wherein the hybrids are fertile. Recent phylogenetic research proposes that the Morus genus should be classified into eight species, including M. alba, M. nigra, M. notabilis, M. serrata, M. celtidifolia, M. insignis, M. rubra, and M. mesozygia.

Based on the search results, here's what is known about the phylogenetic relationships of these families within Rosales:

## Overall Structure

Rosaceae is sister to all other members of the order Rosales, making it the basal family. This leaves the remaining families organized into two major subclades.

## Cannabaceae and Moraceae Relationship

Cannabaceae and Moraceae form a group together (plus Urticaceae), with Ulmaceae as the sister to this combined clade. More specifically, Ulmaceae are sister to Cannabaceae plus (Urticaceae + Moraceae), meaning Moraceae and Urticaceae share a more recent common ancestor with each other than either does with Cannabaceae.

## The Urticalean Rosids Clade

These four families—Cannabaceae, Moraceae, Ulmaceae and Urticaceae—are members of the Urticalean rosids clade within Rosales. These four families form a clade that has strong statistical support in phylogenetic analyses of DNA sequences, informally called the urticalean rosids.

## Methods Used

The phylogenetic relationships were inferred using two nuclear and 10 plastid loci, which provided well-supported results for the interfamily relationships within Rosales.

More specifically, in 1924 Germany was behind in paying reparations required under the Treaty of Versailles, and the Allied nations appointed Dawes to propose ways to restructure that country's financial obligations. Based on the search results, here's the history of when the Wimbledon Championships started:

The first Wimbledon tennis championship opened on July 9, 1877, in an English village about eight miles southwest of London. The championship was held at the All England Lawn Tennis and Croquet Club, with the gentleman's singles competition being the only event held at the time, taking place over nine days.

This inaugural event was organized shortly after Major Walter Clopton Wingfield formalized the rules of lawn tennis in 1873. The championship featured a mere 22 male contestants, and the final match saw W. Spencer Gore defeat William Marshall in front of a crowd of about 200 spectators.

Women were not permitted to compete in the tournament until seven years later. In 1884 the men's doubles competition was introduced and the same year women were also invited to join the tournament.

Wimbledon has since evolved into the world's premier tennis tournament, characterized as the only Grand Slam event played on grass.

**About Bryn Celli Ddu:**
Bryn Celli Ddu, or the 'Mound in the Dark Grove', is a Late Neolithic passage tomb dating to around 5,000 years ago, located in north west Wales, on the island of Anglesey.

**Summer Solstice Alignment:**
The passage into the mound was deliberately aligned so that on the longest day of the year, as soon as the sun rose, it would shine down the passage and illuminate the burial chamber within. It is the only such monument with an association with midsummer solstice sunrise.

The significance to the summer solstice, when the sun rises and shines directly down the passage to illuminate the chamber, was finally proved and documented by the National Museum of Wales in 2005.

An inscribed stone with zig-zags on one side and serpentine patterns on the other was discovered near a ceremonial pit at the back of the chamber.

## Earliest Recording History

In 1927, New York City's Italian Book Company arranged and recorded a version by Sicilian sailor Paolo Citorello (sometimes spelled Citarella), and an American court upheld their copyright in 1928. First recorded in 1927 by baritone Paolo Citorello with the Trio Sciascia, the song draws from Sicilian folk traditions and reflects everyday life and regional humor in early 20th-century southern Italy.

## Song Origins

Related music and lyrics appeared as early as 1835, in the art song "La Danza" (tarantella napoletana) by Gioachino Rossini and Carlo Pepoli. By 1871 in Italy, bawdier versions were circulating.

The song is a comic Sicilian song with worldwide popularity, traditionally styled as a brisk 6/8 tarantella. The song portrays a mother-daughter "coming of age" exchange consisting of various comic, and sometimes sexual, innuendos.

## Later Notable Versions

The song achieved significant international reach through its English-language adaptation, "Lazy Mary," popularized by Italian-American singer Lou Monte in 1958, which became a novelty hit, peaking at #12 on the Billboard Hot 100.

## Establishment Date

Gateway Arch National Park was established on February 22, 2018. President Donald Trump signed the Gateway Arch National Park Designation Act, officially redesignating the Jefferson National Expansion Memorial as Gateway Arch National Park. This made it the 60th national park in the United States.

## Historical Background

The area that is now Gateway Arch National Park was originally designated as the Jefferson National Expansion Memorial on December 21, 1935, through an executive order signed by President Franklin D. Located in St. Louis, Missouri, the park commemorates several significant moments in American history, including the Louisiana Purchase, the Lewis and Clark Expedition, and the nation's growth westward.

The Anti-Slavery Society Convention, 1840 is an 1841 history painting by the British artist Benjamin Robert Haydon. It depicts the World Anti-Slavery Convention, an abolitionist meeting held at the Freemasons' Tavern in London.

Organised by the British and Foreign Anti-Slavery Society, it opened on 12 June 1840. Haydon attended the opening day as a witness after being commissioned by some Quaker attendees to commemorate the event.

Benjamin Robert Haydon, the British history painter, produced a huge 120sq ft canvas with at least 130 recognisable participants. Haydon chose as the moment of his painting the rousing address of the chairman Thomas Clarkson, veteran of the battles against slavery and the slave trade of the eighteenth century.

The painting is now housed at the National Portrait Gallery, London.

The Mock Election is an oil on canvas genre painting by British artist Benjamin Robert Haydon from 1827. It was inspired by a real-life event that took place while Haydon was himself imprisoned at the King's Bench Prison in Southwark for debt.

The inspiration for this subject came from the artist's stay in the King's Bench Prison for Debt in 1827, where prisoners enacted a 'masquerade election' which Haydon watched from his cell. In the picture Haydon includes a number of references alluding to the evils of debt.

The picture was bought by King George IV for £500. Encouraged by this success, he painted a companion picture, Chairing the Member, returning to the prison to make drawings of some of the inmates.

"Chairing the Member" is an 1828 oil painting by British artist Benjamin Robert Haydon. The election subject depicted in the painting relates to a mock election that took place in King's Bench Prison where Haydon was imprisoned for debt, in which prisoners "elected" two Members of Parliament.

Haydon had portrayed the actual voting in his 1827 work "The Mock Election," and for the companion painting "Chairing the Member" he focused on the ceremonial chairing of the winners. 

More details about the prison election: It was proposed that prisoners should elect a member of parliament to represent Tenterden (a slang name for the prison), with three candidates standing for election including Lieutenant Meredith, a veteran of the Peninsula War, and it proceeded like a normal election with candidate addresses, printed placards, and voting.

The painting is an oil on canvas measuring 191.8 cm × 152.4 cm and is located at Tate Britain, London.

The 2017 Cleveland Guardians set the longest consecutive MLB winning streak without a tie with 22 consecutive games from Aug. 24 through Sep. 14. This is the most significant record broken in the 2010s era.

Prior to this, the 2002 Oakland Athletics had won 20 consecutive games, which stood as the modern regular season record before the Guardians broke it in 2017.
